beats.lead: Two records were launched out of the solar system in 1977, and neither one is meant to be played soon
beats.text: Each Voyager probe carries a gold plated copper phonograph record holding sounds and images chosen to represent life and culture on Earth.
beats.note: The contents include 116 images, greetings in 55 languages, and a music selection running from Bach and Beethoven to Chuck Berry and Blind Willie Johnson.

beats.text: The record's cover is inscribed with instructions for playing it, and a sample of pure uranium 238 so that anyone who finds it can date the launch from how much of it has decayed.
beats.note: Uranium 238 has a half life of about 4.5 billion years, so the clue is built to still work long after any human record of the mission is gone.

beats.context: Roughly how long it will take Voyager 1 to pass within a light year and a half of another star, Gliese 445, the record's first close encounter with anything.

beats.lead: One track on the record carries its own small myth
beats.text: Producers wanted the Beatles' Here Comes the Sun on it, and the band agreed, but the record label that controlled the rights would not clear it in time.
beats.note: Accounts of exactly why differ in the details, so this is included as the broad, agreed shape of the story rather than a precise quote.

beats.text: Humanity's message to the universe is more likely to be read by nobody for tens of thousands of years than by anybody at all.

beats.line: The furthest object humans have ever built is still carrying a mixtape.
